answer.exemplar: The method has four steps, and each of them is a statement about one axis rather than about the whole motion. First resolve the launch, which at ${v} m per s and thirty degrees gives a horizontal component of ${vxs} m per s and a vertical component of ${vys} m per s, and it is worth writing both down before starting because they are used repeatedly. Second, find the time of flight, and this uses the vertical axis only: the ball leaves the ground and returns to it, so the time is twice the vertical component over the acceleration of gravity, which is ${Ts} s, and a student who finds half that has found the time to the peak rather than the whole flight. Third, find the range, which is the horizontal component multiplied by that time, ${Rgood} m, and the reason the horizontal component is usable as a constant is that gravity has no horizontal part. Fourth, find the greatest height, which again uses the vertical axis alone, since the vertical component is reduced to zero at the peak, giving the square of the vertical component over twice the acceleration, ${Hs} m. The checks are as important as the arithmetic. The range must come out the same whether it is computed as the horizontal component times the time or from the closed formula with the sine of twice the angle, and those two routes are independent enough that agreement is real evidence. The peak height must be less than the range for a launch of this angle, and the time to the peak must be half the total flight time. A sign convention should be stated at the start, with upwards positive, so that the vertical component at impact comes out negative and the fall is obvious rather than surprising.

questions.explanation: A good answer sets out a method rather than a single result, and it should name the quantity that each step depends on. The launch has to be resolved into a horizontal component that never changes and a vertical component that is reduced steadily by gravity, and that single sentence contains the whole of the independence that makes the topic tractable. The time of flight then follows from the vertical axis alone, being twice the vertical component over the acceleration because the ball must return to the height it left, and the range follows from the horizontal component multiplied by that time. The greatest height follows from the vertical axis again, as the square of the vertical component over twice the acceleration, because that is where the vertical component vanishes. The checks are what separate a careful answer from a lucky one: the range must agree between the component route and the closed formula, the time to the peak must be half the flight time, and the peak height must be smaller than the range for a moderately steep launch. A good answer also states a sign convention before starting, since almost every error in this topic is a sign error in the vertical component.
questions.hint: Resolve the launch first, then use only the vertical axis for the time and the height, and only the horizontal axis for the range.
